note: Tests tool-generated compliance assessments against expert judgement and finds only partial alignment, a caution for automated audit shortcuts.
title: Simplifying software compliance: AI technologies in drafting technical documentation for the AI Act
explain_beginner: The European AI Act requires companies to prepare detailed technical documents for certain AI systems. This is hard because it needs both legal and technical knowledge, which few people have, and small companies may struggle with the cost. This study tested whether AI tools like ChatGPT and a compliance tool called DoXpert can help find missing information in existing documents. Legal experts checked the tools' answers. The tools only partly matched expert views, and ChatGPT had important problems. DoXpert did better, with a moderate link to expert judgments. The takeaway is that AI can help but should not replace human review.
explain_business: New EU rules require technical documentation for high-risk AI, and meeting them can be costly, especially for smaller firms. This study tested AI tools as a shortcut for checking compliance documents. Expert review showed the tools only partly agreed with human specialists. ChatGPT had significant problems, while DoXpert showed a moderate, statistically significant link to expert judgments. The practical implication is that AI can assist compliance work and lower some costs, but it cannot replace expert oversight. Decisions about adopting such tools should include human review and not rely on automated audits alone.
explain_practitioner: The authors examined whether AI tools can identify gaps in technical documentation for the EU AI Act. They used open-source high-risk AI systems as case studies and compared tool-generated compliance assessments with legal experts' judgments. ChatGPT versions 3.5 and 4 showed important issues, while DoXpert had a moderate and statistically significant correlation with expert opinions based on Rank Biserial Correlation analysis. The alignment was only partial overall. The results suggest AI can support human analysis and reduce compliance effort, but automated assessments are not yet reliable enough to stand alone.
